Search works. Let me gather sources.I found sources for all eight verses. Not every tradition is covered, though. The Reformed and Baptist teachers (Gill, Spurgeon, Matthew Henry), the Methodist Adam Clarke and the evangelical sources are well represented. I found nothing from Lutheran, Pentecostal (except Guzik on enduringword.com), Orthodox or prosperity/word-of-faith/hyper-grace teachers on this psalm. Several of my later searches were cut off by a usage limit, so those gaps mean "not found," not "nothing exists."

## Introduction / authorship
- Gill: most think David wrote it when he came to the throne, probably between ruling Judah and ruling all Israel. He also notes that Theodoret saw it as Jews giving thanks on their return from Babylon. He reads it as a prophecy of the Messiah's kingdom and of the Gentiles being called. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/138.htm
- Guzik divides it in two: praise for what God has done (vv. 1–3), then confidence for the future (vv. 4–8). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-138/
- Maclaren (Expositor's Bible) divides it into three parts: vv. 1–3, 4–6 and 7–8. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/138.htm
- **Other view:** Ellicott dates it after the exile. He points to the Greek Old Testament's (LXX) added heading "Of Haggai and Zechariah" and suggests Zerubbabel or Nehemiah wrote it, or perhaps someone in the Maccabean period. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-138.html
- S. Conway's homily in the Pulpit Commentary also leans toward Zerubbabel or Nehemiah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/138.htm

## v. 1
- "With all my heart":
  - Guzik: David holds nothing back. "Whole heart" leaves no room for mixed motives. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-138/
  - Gill: this means sincere, not perfect, worship, with every power of the soul involved. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/138-1.html
  - Utley says it is a Hebrew way of saying total dedication. He contrasts David's whole heart with Solomon's divided heart in old age, and says the key is relationship with God, not performance. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-138
  - Conway: when some troubles still remain, believers should let trust mix with thanks so their praise isn't half-hearted. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/138.htm
- "Before the gods": there are several readings.
  - Spurgeon: the false gods of nearby nations. David's singing showed his contempt for them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps138.cfm
  - Gill lists many options: princes, kings, judges, the Sanhedrin, pagan idols, the ark, or angels. He notes that the Greek, Latin, Ethiopic and Arabic translations all read "angels." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/138.htm
  - Ellicott: definitely "the great" or "mighty" (compare Ps 119:46, "before kings"). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-138.html
  - The Pulpit Commentary gives both views: great men, or pagan idols. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/138.htm
  - Guzik thinks David can't have meant actual idols. He offers rulers or judges (compare v. 4) and cites VanGemeren's view that the verse is a witness against powerless idols. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-138/
  - Maclaren: David vows to sing in the presence of false gods, whose worshippers have no such experience to make them sing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/138.htm
- **Catholic (Augustine):** the Latin says "I will confess to you." Augustine says this is confession of praise, not only of sin, since Christ himself said "I confess to You, Father." He reads the verse as singing "before the Angels." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801138.htm
- **Catholic Bible:** the Douay-Rheims has "in the sight of the angels." https://biblehub.com/catholic/psalms/138-2.htm

## v. 2
- "Toward Your holy temple":
  - Guzik: even away from it, David honoured the temple as God's chosen place of worship. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-138/
  - Gill and the Pulpit Commentary: this means the tabernacle, since the temple wasn't built yet. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/138.htm
  - Gill also sees the tabernacle as a picture of Christ's human nature, the true temple (John 2:19), or possibly heaven. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/138-2.html
  - **Augustine:** the gathering of angels is God's temple. There is a church below (all the faithful) and a church above (all the angels). https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801138.htm
- "Loving devotion and faithfulness":
  - The Pulpit Commentary calls these God's two highest qualities (Exod 34:6), shown in his promises and in keeping them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/138.htm
  - Gill reads them as "grace and truth," which come through Christ (John 1:17). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/138-2.html
- "Your word above … Your name": this is the most debated line.
  - Spurgeon: Scripture outranks every other way God shows himself. Heaven and earth will pass away but God's word will not. Guzik reports that Spurgeon saw the line as the basis for trusting that all of Scripture is inspired. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps138.cfm
  - Guzik: a "stunning" statement. God values his word even above his own name and character. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-138/
  - Spurgeon's collected quotations also offer a second reading: the "Word" is Christ, the eternal Son. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps138.cfm
  - Gill prefers "word of promise and his faithfulness in keeping it," but also allows that it may mean Christ the living Word. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/138.htm
  - Ellicott, the Pulpit Commentary and Maclaren: "word" means the promise. God kept it beyond what his reputation had led people to expect. Maclaren connects it to the promise of David's kingdom. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-138.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-138.html
  - Don Stewart says this should not be read to mean God puts his word above his own character. He notes that modern translations have God exalting both his name and his word above all things. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/stewart_don/faq/the-attributes-of-god-that-belong-to-him-alone/19-does-the-bible-say-that-god-puts-his-word-above-his-name.cfm
  - Constable: God has raised his word equal to his reputation by keeping his promises. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/138-2.html
- **Modern scholarship, text and translation:**
  - Some scholars change the Hebrew to "your truth" (Pulpit) or "your heavens" (Maclaren). Maclaren thinks the text makes sense as it stands. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/138.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-138.html
  - The NET Bible translates "exalted your promise above the entire sky." https://biblehub.com/psalms/138-2.htm
  - Ellicott: the Greek and Latin found the line too hard and put "Thy holy one" in place of "Thy word." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-138.html
  - The Douay-Rheims reads "magnified thy holy name above all." https://biblehub.com/catholic/psalms/138-2.htm

## v. 3
- Guzik sees an order in David's praise: first for who God is, then for his word, then for what God has done. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-138/
- Gill: God answered quickly when Saul was hunting David, and strengthened his faith and courage. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/138.htm
- Spurgeon: strength in the soul means courage and assurance, and it lasts unless a person throws it away through unbelief or pride. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps138.cfm
- Maclaren: the Hebrew "made me bold" literally means "made me proud." Strength welling up inside gave David confidence to face his enemies. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-138.html
- Ellicott offers "encouragest me strongly" and "at my desire." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-138.html
- Conway: the answer came at once and as strength inside, like Paul's "My grace is sufficient." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-138.html
- An older commentary quoted on CCEL's study page (unnamed in what I found): David received fresh strength after being weak and afflicted. https://ccel.org/study/Psalm_138
- **Catholic Bible:** the Douay-Rheims has "thou shalt multiply strength in my soul." https://biblehub.com/catholic/psalms/138-2.htm
- **Augustine** reads it as "multiply me in my soul with virtue," not with cares. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801138.htm

## v. 4
- Guzik: kings will praise God when people who know him tell them his words. He quotes Boice: the verse shows God's people need to be missionaries. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-138/
- Gill: the verb can be read as a wish ("let them praise"). He takes it as kings in the last days coming to Zion and serving the Messiah (Isa 49:23). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/138.htm
- Ellicott: the promise God kept will convince kings. To a Hebrew, "hear Your words" meant the same as "see Your wonders." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-138.html
- Coffman: the kings' thanks rests on hearing how God answered the psalmist's prayer. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/138-6.html
- **A quieter reading (CCEL):** the verse doesn't mean the kings would be converted. It means people everywhere would hear that God had anointed David king. https://ccel.org/study/Psalm_138
- Utley: vv. 4–6 describe what the nations should do. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-138

## v. 5
- Ellicott: "sing of the ways" means God's great works in creation and history. Pagan kings will be made to recognise God's glory. He thinks reading it as kings walking in God's ways goes against the parallel lines. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-138.html
- Gill accepts both "in" and "of" the ways. He finds God's glory in creation and above all in Christ and redemption, spread by the gospel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/138.htm
- Guzik: kings will praise in song because God's glory is great. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-138/

## v. 6
- Guzik connects this to Prov 3:34 / Jas 4:6 / 1 Pet 5:5: God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-138/
- The Pulpit Commentary: God bends down to meet the needs of the lowly, but keeps the proud at a distance "until they are ripe for punishment." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/138.htm
- Barnes: God's greatness doesn't stop him noticing people. The lowly needn't fear being overlooked, and the proud can't hope to escape his eye. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/138-6.html
- Clarke (Methodist): God notices even the smallest part of creation, and especially the humble and afflicted. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/138-6.html
- Ellicott: God looks down on both, with kindness toward the lowly; the proud are simply marked to be kept away. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-138.html
- Gill's "lowly" are those humbled by their sin, who give up trust in their own righteousness and accept Christ's. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/138.htm
- CCEL: our lowliness is no reason to doubt God's fatherly care. https://ccel.org/study/Psalm_138
- Maclaren (historical reading): the lowly one is the psalmist and the proud are his oppressors. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-138.html

## v. 7
- Guzik: thinking about God's greatness and kindness builds the faith that he will revive David. He quotes Trapp: God strikes with the left hand and saves with the right. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-138/
- The Pulpit Commentary lists David's troubles: Saul, foreign enemies, trouble at home. God gave him "a reviving" again and again. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/138.htm
- Gill:
  - Trouble is the road every believer walks.
  - God "revives" by preserving life and stirring up grace.
  - The Hebrew can be "against the nose" of enemies, like checking a horse.
  - The "right hand" may picture Christ.
  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/138-7.html
- Ellicott: this echoes Ps 23:4; 30:3; 71:20. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-138.html
- Maclaren: someone who trusts God may be surrounded by troubles, yet has an inner circle no evil can enter. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-138.html

## v. 8
- Guzik: this is the same as Phil 1:6. It may point to the promise of 2 Sam 7, but it applies to every believer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-138/
- Spurgeon: God cares about everything his servants care about and will complete each part. He outlines the verse as faith's assurance, foundation and prayer. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps138.cfm
- **Perseverance, a Reformed emphasis (Matthew Henry):** our hope of persevering in faith must rest on God's mercy, not our own strength. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_138.cfm
- Maclaren: God never stops until a soul is fully shaped into his likeness. Confidence and prayer are joined here. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/138.htm
- Ellicott:
  - "Will complete for me" (compare Ps 57:2), meaning either "all my undertakings" or what God has begun (Phil 1:6).
  - "Forsake not" means "don't leave them unfinished."
  - The exact meaning depends on when the psalm was written, possibly Nehemiah's rebuilding.
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-138.html
- The Pulpit Commentary: David sees God's care for him as part of God's plan to redeem the world. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/138.htm
- Burgon (quoted by Guzik): God's creating hands, his hands pierced on the cross, and his glorified hands. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-138/
- BibleHub's devotional note: the confidence rests on God's character, not David's performance, yet David still prays because he depends on God. https://biblehub.com/q/What_does_Psalm_138_8_mean.htm
- **Translation:** the NET has "The LORD avenges me" and the NIV "will vindicate me," against "fulfill His purpose." https://biblehub.com/psalms/138-8.htm

## Where traditions differ
I didn't find any real disagreement between Protestant traditions on this psalm in the pages I read. The differences are matters of emphasis:
- **Calvinist Baptist (Gill):** reads Christ and the Gentiles' calling into many verses.
- **Reformed (Henry):** perseverance, in v. 8.
- **Methodist (Clarke):** God's care for the humble, in v. 6.

The real split is between readers who see "word" in v. 2 as Scripture or Christ (Spurgeon, Gill, Guzik) and those who see it as a particular promise that was kept (Ellicott, Pulpit, Maclaren).
